clue.text: Musical group, possibly retro, has to tour clubs

indicators.note: to tour is to travel round, so the scrambled letters go around the clubs letter
'possibly retro' suggests the word retro might be something else, so its letters, with has, are rearranged

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A band with an old-fashioned style must go on a tour of nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' makes ORHESTRA; 'to tour' wraps it round the clubs letter. 'Musical group' also defines the next clue, a palindromic band.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large group of musicians playing together, so it is a kind of musical group.

clue.text: Greek character taking up long and short periods

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking up means reading upwards, so the pieces are written backwards

parts.note: an age is a long period of time
a mo is a moment, a brief while

explanation.surface: A person in a Greek story uses up both long and brief stretches of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'long' and 'short' share 'periods': AGE (a long one) and MO (a short one).
explanation.definitionFit: This is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so a Greek character.

clue.text: Parts of an organ in church bear cracks — that's about right

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go about, around, the letter for right
the word bear cracks, breaking up and rearranging

explanation.surface: Pieces of a church organ, and a bear breaks it; that is about right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' looks musical but is the brain. 'cracks' makes REBA, and 'about' wraps that round the right letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The two cerebral hemispheres are the main parts of the brain, a bodily organ.

clue.text: Islamic ruler of supreme erudition

indicators.note: the letters are taken from within the words that follow, made of them

explanation.surface: A Muslim leader of the highest learning.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a variant spelling of emir, a Muslim prince or commander.

clue.text: Give up one's dinner hour with pained expression, sheep being passed round

indicators.note: the sheep is passed around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: a tup is a ram
ow is a cry of pain

explanation.surface: Someone abandons the lunch hour grimacing as sheep are handed round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give up one's dinner' looks like skipping a meal; it means vomiting.
explanation.definitionFit: To vomit is to bring back up what one ate, hence surrender one's meal.

clue.text: Share totally exaggerated, people claimed

parts.note: all means wholly, totally

indicators.note: the exaggerated piece claims the people, taking them inside

parts.note: OTT, over the top, means exaggerated
men are people

explanation.surface: Someone claims a share was wildly overstated.
explanation.walkthrough: OTT is British shorthand for 'over the top'.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is a portion allotted to someone, their share.

clue.text: Musical group, possibly retro?

indicators.note: retro hints at reading backwards; the name of the band reads the same in either direction

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A question about whether a band might be old-fashioned, echoing the clue before it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Swedish pop group's name is a palindrome, so 'retro' (backwards) leaves it unchanged. The puzzle's theme is this group's songs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish quartet behind many 1970s hits is a famous pop band, so a musical group.

clue.text: A singer shortly going north, south of a Canadian province

indicators.note: in a down clue, south of means placed below, so the other piece comes after
in a down clue, going north means read upwards, backwards
shortly means cut short, losing the final letter

parts.note: a treble is a boy singer with a high voice

explanation.surface: A singer travels north, south of a Canadian province.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' cuts TREBLE to TREBL; 'going north' turns A TREBL into LBERTA, then 'south of' puts it below A.
explanation.definitionFit: This prairie province, capital Edmonton, is one of Canada's ten provinces.

clue.text: Primarily counterpanes observed being spread out?

definitions.text: Primarily counterpanes observed being spread out?

indicators.note: letters spread out are laid out afresh, rearranged
primarily means first, so the opening letter of counterpanes is taken

explanation.surface: Mostly counterpanes are seen spread across a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: counterpanes are things seen spread out over beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Counterpanes are bedspreads, laid out flat across the top of a bed.

clue.text: Honey Honey, Mamma Mia!

parts.note: honey is a term of endearment, like sweetheart
the same endearment repeated

explanation.surface: Two of the band's song titles, Honey Honey and Mamma Mia, set side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: Both phrases are song titles by the themed band, but here 'Honey' is just an endearment and 'Mamma Mia!' an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of dismay or surprise, an Italian one and its mild English equivalent.

clue.text: Urge party to take a fifth of 6 across's number?

parts.note: Lib is short for the Liberal party
the band's song is titled I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do, so one fifth of it is one 'I do'

explanation.surface: A political party is urged to adopt part of a pop song.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do' repeats its phrase five times; one fifth gives I DO.
explanation.definitionFit: Libido is sexual desire or drive, a strong urge.

clue.text: Babble as baby, Dancing Queen!

indicators.note: letters that are dancing move about, so the word baby is rearranged

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: Someone talks baby-talk while singing along to Dancing Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing Queen' is one of the themed band's songs, but here it splits into an anagram signal and ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Yabber is Australian slang for chatter, so babble is a synonym.

clue.text: 6 across's great loss

definitions.meaning: a crushing defeat, after Napoleon's final battle

explanation.surface: A comment that the band suffered a big defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's final defeat in 1815 gave the language its word for any decisive downfall; it is also the band's breakthrough song.

clue.text: Before 1002, I diminish in value

indicators.note: the letter I stands ahead of the other piece, so it comes first

parts.note: 1000 is M in Roman numerals and 2 is a pair

explanation.surface: Someone worries their worth will fall below a certain number.
explanation.walkthrough: 1002 splits as M (Roman thousand) plus PAIR (two).
explanation.definitionFit: To impair something is to damage or weaken it, lessening its worth.

clue.text: Old travelling merchant bringing old stuff over — that's the name of the game!

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upwards, reversed

parts.note: to cram is to stuff
polo is a game; The Name of the Game is also a song by the band

explanation.surface: A merchant from long ago brings his old wares across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Name of the Game' is a song by the band; here it names a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian trader travelled to China in the 13th century, a famous medieval explorer.

clue.text: Song written up about topless prude in mythical kingdom

indicators.note: the reversed song goes about the other piece, enclosing it
in a down clue, written up means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: an air is a song or tune

indicators.note: topless means its top, its first letter, is removed

parts.note: a puritan is a strait-laced, prudish person

explanation.surface: A song is composed about a prude going topless in a fairy-tale realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written up' makes RIA and 'topless' leaves URITAN; 'about' puts the second inside the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Hope's fictional Central European kingdom, setting of The Prisoner of Zenda, is an imaginary realm.

clue.text: Lunatic pleased to accommodate one bright group of relatives?

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room inside, so the scrambled letters take in the numeral
a lunatic arrangement is a crazy one, so the letters of pleased are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A madman is delighted to put up a clever family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunatic' scrambles PLEASED into PLEADES; 'to accommodate' puts I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The star cluster is known as the Seven Sisters, a shining group that are relatives in name.

clue.text: A shade raised around stack

indicators.note: one piece goes around the other, enclosing it

parts.note: to raise animals is to breed them, past tense bred
a rick is a stack of hay or straw

explanation.surface: A ghost lifted up around a chimney stack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shade' looks like a ghost, but it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: This reddish-brown colour, like fired clay, is one shade among many.

clue.text: All passengers in Italy, Charles and Bill

parts.note: Carlo is the Italian form of Charles
an ad, advertisement, is a bill or poster

explanation.surface: Everyone aboard in Italy, including Charles and Bill.
explanation.definitionFit: A full vehicle's load of people is everyone riding in it at once.

clue.text: Mr O'Connor hasn't the talent to be a singer

parts.note: Des O'Connor was a British TV entertainer whose singing was a running joke
can't means is unable to

explanation.surface: A dig that Des O'Connor lacks the gift to be a vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: Des O'Connor was a British TV host and crooner, famously mocked by comedians Morecambe and Wise for his singing.
explanation.definitionFit: The descant is the high voice part above the melody, so its performer, loosely a singer.

clue.text: Keyboard operator extremely twitchy, something of a nut?

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
only something of the nut is used, its first part, the rest dropped

parts.note: the pistachio is a green nut

explanation.surface: A nervy, slightly nutty office worker at a keyboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes T and Y from twitchy; 'something of' cuts PISTACHIO to PIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who types documents works at a keyboard, so operates one.

clue.text: Qualification is secured by college official — no way!

indicators.note: secured by means held inside the other piece
no way means the street abbreviation, ST, is removed

parts.note: a provost heads some colleges

explanation.surface: A qualification is held by a college official who refuses it outright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no way' looks like a refusal; it removes ST (street, a way) from PROVOST to leave PROVO.
explanation.definitionFit: A proviso is a condition or stipulation attached to an agreement, a qualifying clause.

clue.text: 6 across's number outlining case for the inquirer

indicators.note: to outline something is to go around its edge, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: SOS is a 1975 hit by the band
a crate is a packing case

explanation.surface: A band's song is wrapped around a container for someone asking questions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outlining' wraps the band's distress-call song round the case.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian philosopher taught by relentless questioning, so he is the great inquirer.

clue.text: Drunk first of brandies — take a chance on me!

indicators.note: only the opening letter of brandies is taken

parts.note: a lottery game invites you to gamble on it; also a song by the band

explanation.surface: A drinker downs the first brandy and pleads for a chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a Chance on Me' is a song by the band; here it describes a game of chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotto is British slang for extremely intoxicated.

clue.text: Customer taking massage the wrong way, you getting squeezed?

indicators.note: you are squeezed into the other piece
taken the wrong way means read backwards

parts.note: a rub is a massage
ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: A client gets a botched massage that leaves them squeezed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' makes BUR, and 'getting squeezed' presses the old form of you inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A purchaser is someone who pays for goods, a customer.

clue.text: Match captivating a US author

indicators.note: captivating means taking captive, holding inside

parts.note: a twin is a match, an exact counterpart

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture enthrals an American writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain, creator of Tom Sawyer, was a celebrated American novelist.

clue.text: Drink, last bit dropped on envelope

indicators.note: the final letter of the drink is lost

parts.note: cocoa is a hot chocolate drink

explanation.surface: A drink, with its final drop spilt on an envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'envelope' is a noun here, a wrapping, not stationery.
explanation.definitionFit: A silk casing spun by a larva wraps it completely, so it is a protective envelope.

clue.text: Peculiar play with Act 1 at sea

indicators.note: being at sea is being confused, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An odd drama in which the first act is set on the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Something atypical is unusual or out of character, hence odd.

clue.text: PM's first words got Fernando confused with Ring Ring?

indicators.note: something confused is jumbled, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O
a second ring gives another O

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister begins by muddling two of the band's songs, Fernando and Ring Ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PM' looks like the Prime Minister but means post meridiem, after noon.
explanation.definitionFit: This greeting is what one first says to someone once noon has passed.

clue.text: See 26
